title: Why are we doing this?
content:
Why are we doing this? # One page, before any terminal.
You can now build real software by describing it — what people call vibe coding: you say what you want, a model writes it, you steer. It works, startlingly well. And it has a failure mode everyone who tries it eventually hits: three weeks in, neither you nor the model remembers why anything is the way it is. The code is there; the reasoning evaporated with the chat window it happened in.
Deliberative programming is vibe coding made sustainable. The fix is almost embarrassingly simple: decisions get written down, in the repository, as they’re made — each one a small record (“we chose A over B because…; here’s what would change our mind”) that both you and every future model session can find, check, and build on. The records live in git like everything else. No database, no service, no app: files, found by grep, versioned by commits.
Around that simple core there’s now a toolkit — skills and plugins for Claude Code, a VS Code extension that turns the records into something you can read and answer like mail, templates that give a new project the right shape from minute one.
This guide sets you up with your first project. By the end you’ll have: a working development environment (Chapter 2), and a real project — a small game, live on the internet — built with a model collaborator, with your first decisions on the record (Chapter 3). The point isn’t the game. The point is that when you reopen the project next month, the why will still be there.
A note on honesty: you’re among the first people to walk this guide. Where it doesn’t match what you see, that’s not you failing the guide — it’s the guide failing you, and we want to hear about it (every step has a “this doesn’t match” link; it takes ten seconds).

title: Chapter 2 — Setting up your tools
content:
Chapter 2 — Setting up your tools # macOS path. Windows readers: tentative notes are marked — we haven’t walked them end-to-end yet, and we’d genuinely value your corrections ( open an issue with the step ID). Budget 30–45 minutes, mostly waiting on installers. This chapter opens by installing the helper — so every later step has someone to ask.
Each tool below comes with its why — not as filler, but because “install these five things” with no reasons is exactly the context-free instruction style this whole methodology exists to replace.
The terminal ~4 min ☰ Everything in this guide happens in a terminal — and so does the collaborator you’re about to install, which is the real reason to start here: it’s the interface models are most fluent in, where everything they do is a line of text you can read. A terminal is a conversation with your computer in text: you type one line in its language, press Enter, and it answers. It’s the oldest interface computers have — and still the densest: things that take seven clicks and two menus are one line here. More to the point for this guide: it’s the interface your model collaborators are most fluent in. When they work, every action they take is printed as a line of text — in the same language you’re about to start learning.
Open it: ⌘-space, type “Terminal”, Enter. A window appears with a line of text ending in % — the prompt. That’s the computer, waiting.
Five facts, enough to not be lost:
One line at a time. Type, Enter, read the answer, new prompt. Copy-pasting a command from a guide is not cheating — it’s how everyone does it (reading it first is the habit worth having). Quiet usually means working. Installers often print nothing for a minute. A new prompt is the “done” signal, not silence. Passwords type invisibly. When something asks for your Mac password, nothing appears as you type — no dots, nothing. That’s a security feature, not a freeze. Type it and press Enter. ctrl-C abandons a running command and gives the prompt back. It’s the universal “never mind” — you cannot break anything with it that matters. “Open a new terminal” is a real instruction (⌘-N). A terminal reads its configuration once, at birth — so a tool installed a minute ago often exists only in windows opened after the install. When a step says “open a new terminal,” that’s why. Try it:
echo hello What each word does ↕ echo — print back whatever follows. hello — the text to print. It answers hello. You’ve now run a command. Everything else in this guide is this same move, with longer sentences.
✓ You know it worked when: a terminal is open, and echo hello prints hello back
Windows notes are tentative — if you walk this on Windows, tell us what you found.
This doesn't match what I see →
Claude Code ~6 min ☰ Builds on: The terminal
Claude Code is a model who can read files, run commands, and edit code, in a session you steer from the terminal. We install them first on purpose: they need nothing your Mac doesn’t already ship — and everything below this line, they can now help you through, including any step of this guide that goes wrong. Wedging with no one to ask is the old world; you just left it. Paste into the terminal:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash What each word does ↕ curl — the standard download-from-a-URL tool (your Mac ships it). -f — fail quietly on server errors instead of saving an error page. -s / -S — silent (no progress bar), but do show a message if it fails. -L — follow redirects. the URL — Anthropic’s official installer script. You can open it in a browser and read it before running it — that’s not paranoia, that’s the habit this guide is teaching. | — the pipe: feed the left side’s output straight into the right side’s input. bash — run what arrives. You’ll meet this exact download-then-run shape again in a few minutes, installing Homebrew. The different ways — there are several legitimate installs, and this guide recommends exactly one. The others are listed so that when you meet them in the wild, you know they’re the same program:
The native installer (above — recommended, and the guide’s one path): needs nothing but what your Mac already ships, and it keeps itself updated in the background. Homebrew (brew install --cask claude-code): fine — but you don’t have Homebrew yet (next step), and this install doesn’t update itself; you’d have to remember brew upgrade. npm (npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code): for people who already live in Node (version 22+). Under the hood it delivers the same native program as the installer above. [Windows — tentative] In PowerShell: irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex — or winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode.
Then open a new terminal (fact 5!) and run claude once, in any folder: they’ll walk you through logging in with your Anthropic account — the same one you’ve been using in class all semester, which is verified to work. (Reading this from outside the course? Claude Code needs a paid Claude plan or API access — the free plan doesn’t include it; check current pricing before this step.)
One honest note: this is the single step of the guide where nobody can help you yet — you can’t be rescued by the thing you’re installing. That’s exactly why it’s the carefullest page here, and why the one recommended path is the one with the fewest moving parts. If it does fail: the error message is the clue, the “this doesn’t match” link below takes ten seconds, and Anthropic’s own troubleshooting page matches errors to fixes.
✓ You know it worked when: claude --version answers, and claude opens a session that responds
Windows notes are tentative — if you walk this on Windows, tell us what you found.
This doesn't match what I see →
Where Claude Code lives — and why this guide picks the terminal # The same collaborator is reachable from four surfaces: the terminal (what you just installed), a desktop app (the same engine in a graphical shell), a VS Code extension (a panel inside the editor you’ll install later this chapter), and Claude Code on the web (sessions on cloud machines, from a browser). None of them is wrong. This guide teaches the terminal, for three reasons that are really one:
Transparency is the medium, not a feature. In the terminal, everything they do is a printed line — there’s no “view logs” button to find, because the log is the conversation you’re both having. You consent to actions as they happen, in plain sight. What you watch, you inherit. Every command they run is a command you could run yourself; a few weeks of watching is an apprenticeship by proximity. The friendlier surfaces wrap — which means hide — exactly the part you’re here to learn. The collaborator lives in your project. A session starts inside a folder, and that folder — its files, its decision records — is the memory you share. Chapter 3’s whole method is the record lives in the repository; the terminal is the surface where that’s literally visible, not a metaphor behind a pane. And honestly: the other surfaces are easier to learn after the terminal than before it. Learn the unwrapped thing once, and every wrapper becomes obvious.
Your guide, on call — the rule for the rest of this chapter # From this line down, every step of this guide has a diagnostician: if anything wedges — an install that errors, a command “not found,” a password prompt you’re unsure about — open a terminal, run claude, and ask. Paste the exact error; exact beats paraphrased, every time. Something like:
I'm on step setup-homebrew of a setup guide. I ran the install command and got this: [paste the error]. Diagnose it, and tell me what to type — I want to type it myself. That last clause is the rule, and it’s the deal for the rest of this chapter: they diagnose, you type. The tools below are yours — worth installing by your own hand once, because you’ll maintain them for years. (It’s also what keeps every walker of this guide on one shared path: ten people who each let a model improvise a setup end up with ten different machines, and then no step’s verify line means the same thing twice.)
One more thing, so Chapter 3 lands right: what you installed is a helper you can ask. You haven’t recruited anyone yet — reading your project’s mission, consenting to it, taking a name. That’s Chapter 3, and it’s a different, better thing.
Install Homebrew ~8 min ☰ Builds on: The terminal
macOS doesn’t ship a package manager — a single tool that installs, updates, and uninstalls software from the command line. Linux users have had this for decades (it’s the feature that makes a system maintainable rather than a pile of hand-installed apps); Homebrew brought it to the Mac, and nearly everything else in this guide arrives through it in one line each. Paste into the terminal:
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)" What each word does ↕ /bin/bash -c "…" — run the quoted text as a shell script, using the system’s own bash. $( … ) — “replace this with the output of the command inside”: the script is downloaded first, then handed to bash. curl -fsSL — the same four flags, and the same download-then-run shape, as the Claude Code installer you already ran; reading the script first is the same habit. the URL — Homebrew’s official install script, from Homebrew’s own GitHub repository. It will ask for your Mac password (typing shows nothing — that’s normal) and may install Apple’s Command Line Tools first. At the end it prints two echo … >> ~/.zprofile lines under “Next steps” — paste those too.
[Windows — tentative] The closest equivalent is winget (built into Windows 11); choco also works. Tool names below mostly match.
✓ You know it worked when: open a NEW terminal window; brew --version answers
Windows notes are tentative — if you walk this on Windows, tell us what you found.
This doesn't match what I see →
Python, via asdf ~8 min ☰ Builds on: Install Homebrew
Your Mac has a Python, but it’s Apple’s — old, and risky to touch because the system uses it. The real problem asdf solves is versions over time: projects pin different Python (and Node, and more) versions, and asdf lets any number of them cohabit, switching per-project automatically. (Honest note: nothing in this guide invokes Python — this step provisions the rest of the course, where your harness will want it. If you’re racing the clock, it can wait.) brew install asdf echo '. "$(brew --prefix asdf)/libexec/asdf.sh"' >> ~/.zshrc What each word does ↕ brew install asdf — your new package manager’s first job. echo '…' — print a line of text; here, the one-line instruction that loads asdf. >> ~/.zshrc — append it to your shell’s startup file (~ is your home folder; .zshrc runs every time a terminal opens). The > form would overwrite the file — >> adds to the end, which is why the guide uses it. Open a new terminal, then:
asdf plugin add python asdf install python 3.12.4 asdf global python 3.12.4 What each word does ↕ asdf plugin add python — teach asdf about a language: a plugin is asdf’s adapter for one tool family (here, Python). asdf install python 3.12.4 — download and build that exact version; it lives alongside any others, not instead of them. asdf global python 3.12.4 — make it the default everywhere (global), until a project folder says otherwise with a local pin. (The install compiles; a few minutes of scrolling text is expected — fact 2 from the terminal step applies.)
[Windows — tentative] asdf is Unix-only; the spiritually closest path is winget install Python.Python.3.12 — or WSL2, where everything in this guide works as written.
✓ You know it worked when: python --version says 3.12.4
Windows notes are tentative — if you walk this on Windows, tell us what you found.
This doesn't match what I see →
Visual Studio Code ~4 min ☰ Builds on: Install Homebrew
The editor where your project’s files, terminals, and the decision records you’ll meet in Chapter 3 all live in one window. Not the only good editor — but the one this guide’s screenshots show, and the one with the extension we rely on. brew install --cask visual-studio-code Then once: ⌘-shift-P in VS Code → type “shell command” → Install ‘code’ command in PATH. That gives your terminal the code . trick: open any folder as a project.
✓ You know it worked when: in a terminal, code --version answers
This doesn't match what I see →
A fast terminal: Alacritty (optional, recommended) ~3 min ☰ Builds on: Install Homebrew
You’re about to spend real time in a terminal, and snappiness compounds — Alacritty is one of the fastest terminals there is, and it has tabs now, which removes the old reason to skip it. (Entirely optional: Terminal.app and VS Code’s built-in terminal both work for everything in this guide.) brew install --cask alacritty ✓ You know it worked when: it launches; echo hello works like anywhere else
This doesn't match what I see →
Command-line tools: gh and just ~4 min ☰ Builds on: Install Homebrew
gh is GitHub’s own command-line client. Chapter 3 uses it to create your project from a template and connect it to your account without ever leaving the terminal — and once you’re logged in with it, every model collaborator you work with can use it too (creating repos, opening issues) on your behalf, with your consent per action. just is a tiny command runner the template relies on — a menu of named recipes per project; you’ll run your first one at the end of Chapter 3. brew install gh just gh auth login Pick GitHub.com → HTTPS → login with a web browser, and follow the code it gives you. (No GitHub account yet? Chapter 3 step P1 covers signing up — do that first, then come back for gh auth login.)
✓ You know it worked when: gh auth status shows your username, logged in; just --version answers
This doesn't match what I see →
VS Code extensions ~4 min ☰ Builds on: Visual Studio Code
Two small additions make the decision records of Chapter 3 first-class citizens in your editor: ADRs for AI renders them, collects every open question into one view, and lets you answer in place; Terminals Manager relaunches your project’s model sessions in one click (you’ll meet that at the end of Chapter 3). In VS Code, ⌘-shift-X, search and install:
ADRs for AI (publisher: jlumbroso) — or from a terminal: code --install-extension jlumbroso.adrs4ai Terminals Manager (fabiospampinato) — or: code --install-extension fabiospampinato.vscode-terminals Environment complete. Chapter 3 is where it becomes a project.
✓ You know it worked when: ⌘-shift-X → “Installed” lists both
This doesn't match what I see →

title: Chapter 3 — Your first project
content:
Chapter 3 — Your first project # A real project: a Wordle variant, live on GitHub Pages, built with a model collaborator — and your first decisions on the record. Budget ~60 minutes; each step shows its own estimate, and your actual times are something we genuinely want to hear about. One path; each step says how to verify it worked.
A GitHub account ~4 min ☰ GitHub is where your project’s code, its decision records, and (in a few steps) its live website all live. If you already have an account, enter your username below and skip to P2. Go to github.com/signup. Don’t stall on the username — you can change it later (Settings → Account), add or swap email addresses, all of it. Pick something and move.
Then tell the guide who you are — this stays in your browser and personalizes every command below:
Your GitHub username ✓ You know it worked when: you can log in at github.com, and your username is saved below (it personalizes the rest of this guide)
This doesn't match what I see →
Log the tools in ~2 min ☰ Builds on: A GitHub account, Command-line tools: gh and just
The gh tool from Chapter 2 acts as you — so it has to know who you are. This connects the command line to the account you just made. If you skipped the login during Chapter 2’s Command-line tools step (no account yet), now:
gh auth login Pick GitHub.com → HTTPS → login with a web browser, and follow the code it shows you.
What each word does ↕ gh — GitHub’s command-line client (installed in Chapter 2’s Command-line tools step). auth — its authentication command group. login — start a new login: it opens github.com in your browser, shows you a one-time code to type there, and stores the resulting credential locally so every later gh command acts as ⟨github-username⟩. ✓ You know it worked when: gh auth status shows your new username
This doesn't match what I see →
Your repository, from the template ~3 min ☰ Builds on: A GitHub account
The methodology ships as a template repository — a project pre-shaped for working with model collaborators (the decision-record folders, the house rules, the terminal recipes). Template, not fork: your copy starts its own history, owned by you. Go to github.com/ADRs4AI/human-ai-collaboration-template-A, press the green Use this template button (top right — it appears once you’re logged in; the screenshot below shows the page before login, where the green Code button sits in its place) → Create a new repository → name it — wordle-with-records is the name this guide uses below, but it’s yours:
Your repository name → Private is fine → Create.
✓ You know it worked when: your browser is on your new repository’s page, and the file list shows docs/, CLAUDE.md, justfile
This doesn't match what I see →
Clone it, open it ~3 min ☰ Builds on: Your repository, from the template, Visual Studio Code
The repository needs to be on your machine, open in your editor, with a terminal in its folder — that trio is the working posture for everything that follows. gh repo clone ⟨github-username⟩/⟨project-name⟩ cd ⟨project-name⟩ code . What each word does ↕ gh repo clone — copy a repository from GitHub to this machine, wired up so pushes go back to it. ⟨github-username⟩/⟨project-name⟩ — whose repository, and which one. cd ⟨project-name⟩ — move this terminal into the folder the clone just created (change directory). code . — open VS Code on the current folder (. means “right here”), so the editor sees the whole project. Then, inside VS Code: open the built-in terminal (ctrl-backtick). That terminal is already in the project folder — it’s where the next steps happen.
✓ You know it worked when: VS Code shows the project files on the left; ls in its terminal shows CLAUDE.md
This doesn't match what I see →
Recruit your collaborator — mission and project, one paste ~12 min ☰ Builds on: Clone it, open it, Claude Code
This is the step that makes the project different from a chat window. You’re not summoning a tool — you’re recruiting a collaborator into a mission, and the difference is enacted, not poetic: they read the mission first, consent to it, and pick their own name. The paste below carries the mission AND the project, so one message starts everything. In the VS Code terminal, run claude. First launch in a new folder asks setup questions — trust the folder (yes — it’s your own repository), and project MCP servers (enable is fine).
Then paste this — the mission and the project together, one message (edit the project half freely; it’s yours):
Hello — I have a mission for you: my first deliberatively-built project. Read CLAUDE.md and tell me if you accept — any pushback welcome. If you accept: configure the template (the ⟦⟧ placeholders and whatever else it asks), introduce yourself, and then we start on this: The project is a Wordle variant — guess the word, colored feedback per letter — with a twist: the answers are computer science words (ARRAY, STACK, QUEUE, CACHE, TOKEN…). I want it hosted free on GitHub Pages, built with Vue using scoped CSS so styles stay component-local. Before you write any code: what are the 2–3 decisions we should settle first? Put them to me as proper QST cards in the record — with your recommendation on each. They’ll read, decide, name themselves, fill the template’s placeholders (asking you for anything that’s genuinely yours to answer), commit the configuration — and then turn to the project.
✓ You know it worked when: your collaborator has a name; CLAUDE.md’s AI line carries it; git log shows their configuration commit
This doesn't match what I see →
The questions come back ~5 min ☰ Builds on: Recruit your collaborator — mission and project, one paste
A good first ask carries the what and leaves the how open — which is why your paste asked for decisions, not code. What returns is the methodology’s native move, and it’s worth reading slowly the first time. What comes back will look something like this (a real emission from this exact blurb — yours will differ, and should):
QST-VUE-SHAPE: single-file Vue from a CDN, or a Vite build with an Actions deploy? # Status: unanswered Why asking: “Vue with scoped CSS on GitHub Pages” hides a real fork — scoped CSS is a single-file-component feature, and SFCs want a build step. Options:
A — One index.html, Vue from a CDN: no build, push and it’s live. But “scoped” CSS becomes a naming convention we keep by discipline. B — Vite project + GitHub Action deploying to Pages: true scoped styles, the standard modern path. Costs one workflow file. Recommendation: B. Rationale: the project’s own stated constraint is scoped CSS — A quietly downgrades it from a language feature to a promise. Confidence: 0.7. If wrong: if the Actions setup eats more than ~15 minutes, A ships tonight and B becomes a recorded follow-up.
Notice what that is: options you can weigh without leaving the block, a committed position, and the fact that would change it. Questions like these — usually two or three — are now sitting in your docs/adr/ folder, waiting for you.
✓ You know it worked when: your collaborator answered with QST cards, not code — each carrying options, a recommendation, and an If wrong: line
This doesn't match what I see →
Your first answers, four ways ~12 min ☰ Builds on: The questions come back, VS Code extensions
Each card has a recommendation: their pick, the reasoning, a confidence, and (read this part twice) an If wrong: line naming what would change their mind. That last line is the heart of the method: a position stated so it can be checked, not performed so it can be believed. You are the decider; the cards protect your attention — because the reasoning is on the page, agreeing costs you two words. Answer each of your cards a different way, on purpose, to see that the record doesn’t care where answers come from:
In the extension: click the ADRs-for-AI icon in VS Code’s sidebar — open questions appear as a list; open one, read the recommendation, type your answer in the ANS box. (“A, agreed.” is a complete answer when you agree — the why is already on the page. Diverging? Then say why; the slot has no size limit.) Manually: open the ADR file itself, find the next card’s **ANS:** line (the [Fill this in] placeholder marks the blank), and type your answer right in the file. Save. That’s it — the extension and the model read the same file you just edited; there is no database, and now you know it. From your phone: install the GitHub mobile app, open your repository → the ADR file → edit → answer the third card → commit from your thumbs. Decisions don’t wait for your desk. (Pull before the next step: git pull in the terminal.) Notify the seat: back in the terminal, tell your collaborator: “I’ve answered everything — pull, read, and proceed.” Watch what happens: they read your answers from the files, update the records, and start building — no re-explaining, no “as I mentioned above.” The record carried it. ✓ You know it worked when: every QST shows answered (the extension’s list drains to zero), and your collaborator is building
This doesn't match what I see →
Ship it ~10 min ☰ Builds on: Your first answers, four ways
The decisions you made govern the build; this is where they become a thing on the internet with your name on it. Your collaborator builds the Wordle and sets up GitHub Pages deployment (they know how; the decisions you made in P7 govern the details — ask them to walk you through enabling Pages if a browser step needs your click). When they give you a link at ⟨github-username⟩.github.io, open it. Play a round. You built that — the two of you.
✓ You know it worked when: the game loads at your *.github.io URL and a CS word wins a round
This doesn't match what I see →
Tweaks, the deliberate way ~8 min ☰ Builds on: Ship it
The first change after a build is where vibe coding usually starts shedding context. Not here — one more decision, on the record. Pick any tweak you actually want — hard mode, a streak counter, dark theme, more words, a hint system. Ask for it the same way: “I want X — if there’s a real fork in how, QST it; if not, just build.” Small tweaks won’t need a card; one of yours probably will. Answer it whichever of the four ways you liked best. ✓ You know it worked when: the tweak is live, and grep -rn '^### QST' docs/adr/ shows your decisions accumulating — that grep is the whole retrieval system, forever
This doesn't match what I see →
The crew, one click ~4 min ☰ Builds on: Recruit your collaborator — mission and project, one paste
Real projects grow more than one collaborator session, and reopening them one by one gets old. The template ships the cure. In the project terminal:
just refresh-terminals What each word does ↕ just — a command runner the template ships configured; it reads the project’s justfile, a menu of named recipes. refresh-terminals — the recipe that regenerates .vscode/terminals.json: the list of model-collaborator terminals this project knows how to reopen. …then ⌘-shift-P → Terminals: Run. Every configured session launches at once. Tomorrow, when you reopen this project: code ., one Terminals: Run, and the crew is back — reading the same records you and they wrote today, remembering why everything is the way it is.
That’s the guide — and you’re among the first to walk it: your stall points are worth more to us than your successes.
✓ You know it worked when: Terminals: Run opens your collaborator’s terminal(s) automatically
This doesn't match what I see →

title: Tell us what happened
content:
Tell us what happened # Two minutes, two moves — and if you’re reading this page because you’re stopping partway, that’s exactly as valuable: tell us where and why (ten seconds, three boxes), and thank you — the walkers who stop are the ones a guide learns the most from.
The debrief — a record, like everything else ~5 min ☰ Builds on: Your first answers, four ways
You just practiced putting decisions on the record. The last move is to put the walk itself on the record — and this one is ungraded, and will stay that way: it calibrates the guide, never you. You are among its first walkers; your stall points are worth more to us than your successes. Ask your collaborator:
Before we wrap: please write docs/adr/debrief-first-walk.md — a short record of this first walk, from both of us. Four sections: what we built and the decisions on the record; roughly how long each chapter actually took me; where the guide didn't match what we saw (step IDs if we noted them); and what you'd tell the next pair who walks this. Mark it clearly as ungraded feedback for the guide's authors. Then commit it. Then get it to us, either way is complete:
Share: open a walk report and paste your repository link (private is fine — add jlumbroso as a reader), or Summarize: same form, paste the debrief’s text instead of the link. Keeping your repo to yourself is a fine choice and costs nothing. No GitHub account (you stopped before Chapter 3)? Email works: the course announcement’s reply button, three lines — where you stopped, what it said, what you expected.
✓ You know it worked when: a docs/adr/debrief-first-walk.md exists in your project, and we have either its link or its summary
This doesn't match what I see →

title: Your variables
content:
Your variables # This guide personalizes itself. Two values, entered once, appear in every command that needs them — so what you copy-paste is already yours, not a template you have to patch by hand.
Your GitHub username Your repository name Where they live: in your browser’s local storage, and nowhere else. They never leave your machine, we never see them, and clearing your browser data clears them (the guide then just shows the placeholders again). You can change them here any time and every page updates.
What belongs here — and what never does: these slots hold identifiers — names that are public anyway, like a GitHub username. No step of this guide will ever ask you to enter a password, a token, or an API key into a page — if something that looks like this guide ever does, that’s a bug and a lesson: report it.
Why a guide would bother: half the friction in setup guides is the silent “replace YOUR-NAME-HERE” step — it’s where typos live and where copy-paste confidence dies. Naming the variables, and being explicit about where they’re stored, is the same move this whole methodology makes with decisions: what’s implicit rots; what’s written down can be checked.

title: All tasks
content: Every task in this guide, in order, with its tick. Each links back to its step in context; your checkmarks are the same wherever you tick them.
